newsitem.title: UK: UK's George says does not want restrictive policy.
newsitem.headline: UK's George says does not want restrictive policy.

text.p: Bank of England Governor Eddie George said on Thursday he had no intention of using his new authority to set interest rates unduly restrictively.

In a speech to top City bankers in London's Mansion House, George said the government's new monetary framework -- which leaves the Bank free to set interest rates to meet a revamped inflation target -- made it clear the Bank must aim for a 2.5 percent goal for underlying inflation as a mid-point.

"I am well aware that some observers have been concerned that, in exercising its new responsibility, the Bank will adopt an unduly cautious approach, thereby imparting a restrictive bias to the economy," George said. "That will not be our intention."
Earlier on Thursday, Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown reaffirmed his 2.5 percent target for annual underlying inflation.

But in a letter to George, Brown said that if RPIX -- which excludes volatile home loan payments -- deviated from the target by more than one percentage point in either direction, he would expect a public letter from the Governor explaining why.

Last month, just five days into office, Brown gave the Bank of England operational independence to set interest rates. The Bank flexed its new muscles last Friday, raising base rates by a quarter-point to 6.5 percent.

Critics of Brown's decision to let the Bank set rates had argued that in his zeal to defeat inflation, George would force interest rates higher than was healthy for the economy, leading to job losses and falling output.
But George said: "The measure of our success will be how close we in fact come to 2.5 percent on average over time."

"Operationally it implies that, with a balanced distribution of risk, there should be an even chance of an outturn -- at the end of our two-year forecast horizon -- either above or below 2.5 percent."
George also told his Mansion House audience that there was no contradiction between economic growth and price stability.
Britain's economic performance over the past five years showed "there is no conflict -- certainly no necessary conflict -- between growth and price stability in the medium-term."

The Chancellor's reforms showed he did not share the view that monetary policy aimed at controlling inflation clashed with the wider aims of growth, employment and rising living standards. "Nor, emphatically, do I," George said.

The central bank chief also addressed the third plank of Brown's reforms -- the creation of a new super-regulator for Britain's financial sector, robbing the Bank of its traditional position as overseer of the banking industry.
"Separation of responsibility for banking supervision from central bank responsibility of the overall stability of the financial system as a whole is not, in itself, at all unusual," George said.
But he said there were dangers of one, over-arching organisation becoming too bureaucratic and leading to a "one-size-fits-all" approach.
"Or it could fail to maintain an appropriate balance between its responsibilities for protecting consumers and the need to allow competitive financial markets to breathe," George said.
The key to the success of the new arrangements was for the Bank to preserve close links with the new, all-powerful Securities and Investment Board.
"I have no doubt that we will indeed be able to establish the necessary close relationship...not least because the new super-SIB will be headed by our own Deputy Governor (Howard Davies)," he said.
